segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Welcome to a special ForceFinder briefing. I'm Avery.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: And I'm Cole. Today we're leaving the Middle East and Ukraine aside and looking at our own hemisphere. As always, this is generated automatically from public, open-source reporting, and the sources are listed at the end.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: We'll cover Mexico's cartels, El Salvador's gang crackdown, the crisis in Haiti, and the governments in Venezuela, Cuba and Nicaragua. Then Colombia and Ecuador, and the US strikes on drug boats at sea.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: And one thread ties a lot of it together. Since last year, the US government has designated many of these criminal groups as foreign terrorist organisations. That changes how Washington treats them, militarily and legally.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Let's start with Mexico. The State Department lists the Sinaloa Cartel and the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, known as C J N G, as foreign terrorist organisations, along with several other Mexican groups.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: The biggest event this year was in February. In an operation in Tapalpa, in Jalisco state, Mexican forces killed the C J N G's leader, Nemesio Oseguera, known as El Mencho. Mexico's defence ministry says US intelligence helped locate him.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: But US government assessments say the cartel hasn't broken apart without him. And the Sinaloa Cartel and C J N G factions are still fighting over smuggling routes.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: The US also set up a Joint Interagency Task Force, Counter Cartel, in January, based in Tucson, Arizona. Its job is to identify and dismantle cartel operations along the border. Reuters reports it helped in the hunt for El Mencho.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Mexico's President Sheinbaum, though, rejects any US military action on Mexican soil. And we haven't seen a confirmed US strike inside Mexico.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: The fighting goes on day to day. On November fifth, soldiers killed three armed men near Navolato, in Sinaloa, after coming under fire. And federal forces killed a man known as El General near Mexico City. The US Treasury had sanctioned him last year.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Next, El Salvador. President Nayib Bukele's state of exception has been in place since March twenty twenty-two. More than ninety-two thousand people have been arrested under it.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: The government says homicides have fallen dramatically, and the gangs, including M S thirteen, which the US also designates as a terrorist organisation, have been badly weakened.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: But rights groups point to the cost. Amnesty International documented at least four hundred and seventy deaths in state custody under the state of exception. And in April, prosecutors opened a mass trial of four hundred and eighty-six alleged M S thirteen members.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: In October, Bukele said the government is weighing early, conditional release for roughly half of those held for collaborating with gangs. A commission is reviewing the cases. No timeline yet.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: And that brings us to Haiti, where El Salvador is now directly involved.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: Right. Gang coalitions, mainly Viv Ansanm, control an estimated eighty-five to ninety percent of the capital, Port-au-Prince. The US designated Viv Ansanm and another gang, Gran Grif, as terrorist organisations last year.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: A UN-authorised Gang Suppression Force is there. In September, the Security Council extended its mandate to the end of March twenty twenty-seven. Estimates of its size range from under a thousand to about fifteen hundred troops.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: Then, on October eighteenth, gangs ambushed and kidnapped four Salvadoran aviation technicians serving with that force. Three days later, El Salvador launched its own military intervention. Reports say about two thousand Salvadoran troops have deployed.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: The fate of the four technicians is still unclear. On November second, residents of the Plaine du Cul-de-Sac protested against the Salvadoran operation, reportedly under death threats from Viv Ansanm. And Crisis Group warns the rapid deployment, without a clear chain of command, could fuel more clashes.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: Haiti's government also says Mathias Saintil, who led a gang in Cité Soleil, is dead. That hasn't been independently confirmed.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Let's turn to the governments. Venezuela has changed dramatically this year. On January third, a US military operation captured Nicolás Maduro. He's jailed in New York, with a trial set for June twenty twenty-seven.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: His former vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, now leads an interim government. On November second, Secretary of State Rubio met Venezuela's foreign minister and pushed a three-phase plan: stabilisation, economic recovery, then a democratic transition.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: The New York Times reports the US is negotiating a status of forces agreement, which could allow a long-term US military presence. And a UN fact-finding mission found only limited improvement in human rights, with at least eighty-seven people detained for political reasons since Maduro's capture.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: Cuba is in what analysts call its worst crisis in decades, after Venezuelan oil stopped arriving. Our latest detailed reporting is from May, so this part is a few months old.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: At that point Cuba's energy minister said the island had run out of fuel. There were long blackouts, hospitals suspending surgeries, and rare protests in Havana. President Díaz-Canel blames US sanctions.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: Secretary Rubio has offered a hundred million dollars in aid, on condition it goes through the Catholic Church rather than the government. And there were reports the Justice Department was preparing an indictment of former president Raúl Castro.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Nicaragua is where the human-rights reporting is starkest. In July, President Daniel Ortega said there would be no more competitive elections, extending his rule of nearly twenty years alongside his wife and co-president, Rosario Murillo.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: In September, UN experts said the government was responsible for the deaths in custody of eight political detainees, and had, in their words, weaponised enforced disappearance. Human Rights Watch counted at least seventy-seven political prisoners as of October.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: And the pressure reaches beyond its borders. In June, Roberto Samcam, a retired army major and Ortega critic, was killed in exile in Costa Rica. Costa Rican authorities detained four people.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: Quickly to the Andes. In Colombia, the US designated the Clan del Golfo as a terrorist organisation last December. On November sixth, a police operation against it in San Martín, in Cesar department, left three dead.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: In Ecuador, the rival gangs Los Lobos and Los Choneros were designated last year. The monitoring group ACLED says their turf war is a key driver of Ecuador's violence.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: And finally, at sea. The US military has carried out a long campaign of strikes on boats it says are smuggling drugs, in the Caribbean and the Eastern Pacific.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: The latest confirmed strike was on October twenty-seventh, in the Eastern Pacific. Southern Command says five people were killed. The Washington Office on Latin America counts at least two hundred and thirty-eight people killed in sixty-eight strikes, and critics question whether the campaign is legal or effective.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: So, what to watch. Whether the four Salvadoran technicians are found, and whether El Salvador's operation in Haiti changes the fight against the gangs.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Whether the US and Venezuela sign that military agreement. Whether Mexico's cartels splinter further after El Mencho. And whether Washington takes its fight against designated cartels from the sea onto land.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: That's the Western Hemisphere briefing. Thanks for watching.
